summary: Rainprint is an interactive web application that shows which areas of the Cajamarca region (Peru) are most prone to flooding and how much rain each area receives. It combines NASA satellite data (NASADEM terrain, GPM IMERG rainfall and MODIS land cover) with river network and population information, and calculates a susceptibility index in four color categories: low, medium, high and very high. The application lets users switch between the risk map and the annual and December-to-April rainfall maps, query any point with a click, see which months are rainiest and estimate how many people live in high-risk areas. Its purpose is to offer communities, authorities and students a clear, free tool to understand and prevent flood risk.
details:
Executive Summary

Rainprint is a geospatial visualization tool, built with NASA data, that identifies the areas of Cajamarca most susceptible to flooding and shows the region’s rainfall regime. It is designed for non-specialists: it uses colors, plain-language texts and a simple panel.

1.1. What does it do?

Rainprint generates a flood susceptibility map for the 13 provinces of the Cajamarca region. The user can:

•         Choose between three maps: flood risk, rainfall over a year and rainfall from December to April.

•         Show or hide the main rivers, the province boundaries and where people live.

•         Click any point to see its risk level, its elevation and the rainfall it receives.

•         See a chart with the average rainfall for each month.

•         Find out how many people live in high or very high risk areas, in total and by province.

1.2. How does it work?

The application calculates a susceptibility index by combining five factors. Each factor is converted to a scale from 0 (lowest susceptibility) to 1 (highest) and they are added together using the weights shown in the table.

MODIS MCD12Q1 (NASA)

Urban surfaces, wetlands and water contribute more susceptibility than forests

10%

 

The classes are defined by percentiles within Cajamarca: low (the 50% of the region with the lowest index), medium (the next 25%), high (the next 15%) and very high (the 10% with the highest index). To estimate the exposed population, the inhabitants (WorldPop 2020) living in high or very high risk areas in each province are added up.

Rainfall is calculated as the average of the monthly GPM IMERG data between 2001 and 2020.

1.3. Innovation and purpose

Satellite data on terrain, rainfall and land cover are often hard to interpret for non-specialists. Rainprint turns them into an understandable map, with clear legends, plain-language descriptions and click-to-query, without the user having to install anything or need an account. Its purpose is to bring NASA data closer to the people of Cajamarca and to support a culture of prevention.

1.4. Benefits and impact

A. Social, environmental and technological benefits

•         Social: informs communities and local authorities about the most exposed areas and how many people live in them.

•         Environmental: helps people understand how terrain, rivers and rainfall influence risk, and plan land use better.

•         Technological: integrates several open satellite data sources into a single free tool that can be accessed from a browser.

B. Contribution to the Sustainable Development Goals

•         SDG 11, Sustainable cities and communities: reduce the impact of disasters on the population.

•         SDG 13, Climate action: strengthen the capacity to adapt to climate-related risks.

•         SDG 9, Industry, innovation and infrastructure: use technology and open data to solve a local problem.

C. Expected impact on the community

Students, authorities and local organizations are expected to use Rainprint as a starting point to discuss prevention and to identify areas that require more detailed studies. It can also serve as a basis for future research that uses open NASA data.

1.5. Objectives and expected results

General objective: build a web tool that shows flood susceptibility and rainfall in Cajamarca using NASA data.

Specific objectives:

1.       Integrate terrain, rainfall and land cover data into a susceptibility index.

2.       Classify the territory into four risk categories.

3.       Estimate the population living in high-risk areas by province.

4.       Publish the tool with a public link and an interface that non-specialists can understand.

1.7.2. Programming language and framework

JavaScript with the Google Earth Engine API and its interface library (ui).

1.7.3. Hardware and sensors

Personal computers with an internet connection were used. The data come from satellite sensors: the NASA and JAXA GPM mission (rainfall), the SRTM mission (terrain, the basis of NASADEM) and the MODIS instrument (land cover).

1.9. Project location

The project is developed for the Cajamarca region, in northern Peru, which comprises 13 provinces and a terrain of valleys, slopes and highlands with a marked rainy season.

Justification: seasonal rains and settlements near rivers expose many communities to floods and other water-related hazards. Having a clear, free map helps identify where it is worth deepening studies and prevention measures. For example, the El Niño phenomenon in Cajamarca.

1.10. Impact and benefits

Relevance to NASA’s mission and strategic alignment

Rainprint uses products derived from NASA missions and sensors: the GPM mission (global precipitation, with the IMERG product), the SRTM mission (terrain, reprocessed as NASADEM) and the MODIS instrument (land cover). It aligns with the use of open satellite data to understand the water cycle and support disaster risk management, and shows how those data can be applied to a specific region.

1.11. Expected results

•         A flood susceptibility map for the entire region, with four color categories.

•         Annual and rainy-season rainfall maps.

•         An estimate of the population in high or very high risk areas, by province: Cajamarca: 248,802 people

•         A public application, with no account requirements, understandable to non-specialists.

1.12. Conclusions and future improvements

Lessons learned

•         At first we used fixed thresholds to classify risk and the map came out almost uniform, because the terrain in Cajamarca is very steep. We switched to classifying by percentiles and the map showed clear differences between areas.

•         Data with gaps can leave the result empty; they had to be filled before calculating the index.

•         To reach non-specialists, we removed layers and technical terms and kept only what can be understood at first glance.

Limitations

•         It is a susceptibility index, not a hydraulic model: it does not simulate flows or water depths.

•         The categories are relative to Cajamarca: “very high” means the 10% of the region with the highest index, not an absolute level of danger.

•         Satellite rainfall has a resolution of about 10 km and may not capture local variations in mountain terrain.

•         The exposed population is an estimate based on WorldPop 2020.

•         The map has not yet been validated against historical flood records.

Possible optimizations

•         Validate the index with emergency records (for example, from INDECI) and with historical flood data.

•         Incorporate soil moisture (NASA SMAP) and rainfall trend analysis.

•         Add scenarios for especially rainy years and data from SENAMHI stations.

•         Create a static version for GitHub Pages and a mobile version.
